title: The Secret of the River Yamuna
summary: Akbar stands on the riverbank and grieves over the passing of his youth. Birbal uses the flowing current to explain the eternal renewal of existence.
full_text:
On an autumn twilight, Emperor Akbar stood upon the river terrace of the Agra Fort, gazing down at the dark, swirling waters of the Yamuna river. The monarch looked weary and somber, noticing a few silver hairs in his beard and the deepening lines upon his brow.

Akbar sighed deeply: 'Birbal, looking at this river fills my heart with sorrow. Time flows like this river, washing away our youth, our strength, and our companions. In fifty years, I shall be dust in a tomb, and this water will still be flowing past these walls, indifferent to emperors and empires. What is the meaning of all our conquests and glory if time washes everything away?'

Birbal stepped to the stone parapet, dipped a brass bowl into the flowing current, and poured the water slowly back into the river.

Birbal spoke in a gentle, melodious voice:

'Sire, you see the river as a thief of time, but consider the river as the great giver of life!

'The water that flows past your terrace today was snow on the highest peaks of the Himalayas yesterday. Tomorrow, it will irrigate the wheat fields of peasant farmers; next week, it will nourish thirsty cattle; next month, it will join the great ocean, rise as clouds into the heavens, and fall as sweet rain upon your rose gardens once again!

'Nothing in this universe is truly destroyed; life merely changes its form in eternal renewal!

'An emperor does not live forever in his physical flesh, but he lives forever in the justice he established, the schools he built, the peace he protected, and the tears he wiped from the eyes of the poor!

'Do not mourn that the river flows; rejoice that you have been chosen by heaven to build bridges of justice and mercy across its waters while your day lasts.'

Akbar felt a profound peace wash over his spirit. The melancholy lifted from his heart like morning mist before the sun. He embraced Birbal, thanking him for transforming sorrow into sublime purpose.
moral: Life flows like a river; the only constant is change, and clinging to the past brings sorrow.
